"What the hell does that have to do with Vietnam?!" The movie is good at proving a point on everyone not trying to care despite giving effort into making things complicated. I just had a hard time believing Obadiah from Iron Man is just here. As a polar opposite of his role. And that they made Sullivan an unhinged war veteran. I guess that monster energy business didn't work out for him. The "Dude" is the definition of a washed up junkie just doing what he wants to do. He is a bit more self aware of his surroundings and is rational, even if his entire shtick is to be nonchalant.  He clocked the entire conflict on the kidnapping being just a ploy for the hostage, only difference was that the more he engaged with the hijinx of the Lebowski family and their money, the more he fell into a rabbit hole of problems. Walter is also a good example of being too engaged with something to a point where it shouldn't be. He tries to commit to things like being Jewish even if he isn't, sticks to bowling rules like it's the law, and picks fights he has little odds with. He is the reason Dude got stick in the ransom situation and is why it got escalated. The moment the conflict is something that doesn't relate to him or bother him, he disengages and dissacosiates with bowling. The death of their friend and the constant imagery of bowling from Dude's acid trip were also good contrasts to how Dude handles his pressure and his focus on reality. He chooses to associate around the end to what was important now after the money situation died down. And that, despite how much Walter ruined Dude's life, he keeps him as a friend because he no longer wanted to continue caring. In a world where he already tried proving himself, the situation gave him one more reason not to pivot to chaos anymore and stick with his laid back lifestyle. Anyhow this movie also taught me to love my toe more. No sliced toes.

This movie pretty much subverts every expectation you would have going off its premise. It’s very different in how its narrative unfolds, some could receive this as “that’s it?” or “nothing really happens” but I think its structure itself is conducive to what it’s trying to communicate. This movie depicts the absurdity of existence through a very comedic manner which was really compelling. The final monologue of the stranger is also really powerful and reflective. Very enjoyable as well. Solid stuff. It loses a star tho because I heavily disagree with the philosophy it endorses through “the dude”.

Something I love about the Coens is their ability to portray just how strange regular people are. They show this both in how someone really is, the random hills they will die on, their grand goal to in which happiness will be achieved, the creature comforts they enjoy. In addition, how on top of that, the characters society makes us play to each other when interacting and not only how that is odd, but even more odd when people stitch those roles into the fabric of their identity. Obviously in a Coen movie these things are more exaggerated or on the surface, but believe me, really listen to people you know or be more vulnerable with divulging your real thoughts and you’ll see we are all little freaks and that’s awesome. Everyday life is colored with such surrealism. On a side note Walter will go down as one of the performances so good at being a type of person I cannot stand that I had to be like “it’s just a movie it’s just John Goodman”

The Big Lebowski is one of those films that is unapologetically different; quirky and absurd, meandering and carefree, hilarious and ‘slap in the face’ crude at times. It is a film that seems to be ridiculous for the sake of it, but looking a bit deeper, it is almost a conceptual adaptation of the film The Big Sleep and many other old noirs, and it hides an ingenious commentary on a century old film law that will change the way you see it forever. The film is very entertaining throughout the entire two hour showing, and features the classic unique humor of films common before the marvel era. The editing often adds to the hilarity of many moments, –particularly when ‘the Dude’ as Lebowski likes to call himself is drugged or unconscious–but it is low-key for most of the film to match the mood. The film also feels very real, as the Mise-en-sćene is on point, capturing the Dude’s lazy lifestyle in the grubbiness of his house and the favorite bathrobe which he always wears. The music is similarly on point, and the needledrops somehow set the correct mood just about every time. The dialogue is quirky and a little weird sometimes, which admittedly matches the overall vibe of the film, as do the abundant F-bombs permeating the entirety of the show. The story however is the biggest ‘strength’ of the movie if I may be so bold as to call it that. Borrowing from many common tropes of classic noir and mystery films, The Big Lebowski takes them and twists them ingeniously with the anti-hero archetype, to write a story about a deadbeat loser who likes bowling being thrown into a mystery with his life at stake. It is presented well for the most part, and though I'm not a fan of how some of the storytelling is omniscient, the laidback and unhurried feel of the story make up for it. At the very start of the movie, the narrator, when talking about the Dude says “I won’t call him a Hero–Because what is a hero?–but sometimes there’s a man…the man for his time and place” and the rest of the movie struggles with this question, and Dude’s identity as an unlikely hero, ultimately exploring the themes of impermanence, how to abide in an indifferent world, and the virtue of enjoying a simple life. (Bonus: The Hays Code/Adaptation Theory) There is another way to look at The Big Lebowski, which re-contextualizes everything about the way we see it. In adaptation theory, there are three main types of adaptations, Literal, Traditional, and Radical/Analogical. This new way to look at The Big Lebowski sees the film as a radical adaptation of The Big Sleep, a noir film we previously watched. We can see parallels between the two films left and right, but there’s one major difference, the Hays code. The Hays code was a rule in filmmaking implemented in the 1930’s that prohibited the inclusion of any immoral or violent content into the films. The Big Lebowski seems to be a commentary on the Hays code; a loose adaptation of The Big Sleep but without skirting around all the questionable content. For some people this is a massive revelation and changes their entire perspective of the film, and while I love the creative and innovative idea, my perspective on the movie wasn’t drastically altered because of this particular, seemingly random reference. Overall, The Big Lebowski is a good Noir-Parody/Comedy film that loves a good laugh and an F-bomb, with a likable antihero and an interesting story behind its adaptation.

The last scene of this movie leaves me with such comfort. "The Dude Abides." and just Bridges overall energy that he leaves us with even after the whole tirade with the nihilists, a fake millionaire, and a slew of pointless mishaps that all occur due to his name. "Can't worry about that shit. Life goes on, man." Such a simple line, but yet runs do deep. I wanna be on this level of laxed. I kinda just wanna be The Dude. Not necessarily living in this movie per say, but just the Zen and comfortability with his own vessel and just riding out this hellhole called "life". I think it might be the funniest movie of all time on top of all this. Its got great characters, some astonishing framework, an excellent soundtrack, all combined into a plot that has NOTHING to do with the main character. The Dudes life is just rudely interrupted by mistake and his simple life of bowling, driving around, and smoking weed gets put on hiatus all because some ignorant ass people want money. But, like he said. "Can't worry about that shit. Life goes on, man."

I’ve probably seen this a few times too many, and the lore of Lebowski — books, festivals, etc — got a bit much for a while there. But it remains one of my favourites by the Coens, really, when it comes down to it, this and Fargo are the films that stand up the best from the immediate era after they made their name. For me, anyway. I mean, a couple others sure. Of course. But this and Fargo back to back was a top run, really. Watched it again, and my favourite bit in it is the circular passing of language. Characters that are connected by a scene, but not really connected by context, or sometimes not even connected by a scene will pass language between one another. Maude Lebowski introduces The Dude to the word ‘Johnson’ as slang for penis. Then the Nihilists bust into his bathtub and threaten to cut off his Johnson. It’s a great way of positioning The Dude as the conduit this madcap world of screwball comedy is passing through. Superb cast, cameos, and performances. Great soundtrack. I like to think Sam Elliott’s “Stranger” narrator meeting The Dude and interacting, while the Tumbling Tumbleweed song plays, is an oblique reference to the bar in the Overlook in the Shining, when Jack Nicholson’s character says to the barkeep, “I like you Lloyd, I always have”. But then, enough of my yappin

The Dude abides. He doesn’t align with an ideology, he doesn’t classify himself as anything but The Dude. He isn’t deeply opinionated or bound by his roots and his past. He simply does what makes him happy and content. He goes bowling, he smokes weed and most importantly he has his rug which really ties the room together. Throughout the film he is constantly dragged away from his simple life by people of all types of ideologies. The nihilists, the fascists, war veterans, corrupt pornographers and of course the big Lebowski. What connects all these different factions is LA; early 90s LA. The specific time and location where all of these people of strong beliefs congest and complicate life for the dude. He’s simply a tumbleweed in the wind, dragged literally and figuratively into the web of crime and corruption often by Walter. Walter who is constantly exploding into violence yet claims he once dabbled in pacifism. The Coens create such an amusing critique of ideologies using the contrast to the dude. Every other character is driven by money, sex or violence despite what they say. Even Maude and Donny aren’t as pure as the dude as they both seek out sex/money by the end, despite generally being very good characters. The Coens show how nobody truly follows their beliefs and every character contradicts themselves. The Nihilists don’t care about anything yet constantly pursue the ransom money. The big lebowski acts like a successful man yet it’s all a facade to get money in the first place. Then the film takes a turn towards the end as it carries through the character development and commentary from the first half and starts to become an outlook on the human condition. “I guess that's the way the whole durned human comedy keeps perpetuatin' itself down through the generations. Westward the wagons, across the sands of time” . That’s what this film is at its core, a human comedy. Balancing nihilism and cynicism whilst being the funniest and most quotable film of all time.

Has been the 3rd rewatch in about 6 years…tonight reminded me it’s just fucking awesome. The writing is original and clean and smart, and I can’t find any other words for it except just being pleasantly surprised and heavily entertained, every time I chuck it on. And it’s been so well written that you pick up different things from the movie every time. Between being funny without trying, some amazing choreographed shots, mixing in characters that could just be figments of imagination (iykyk), cool dialogue and a classy soundtrack, I genuinely think this is one of my favourite movies of all time. And the character of The Dude I feel like I could watch him or listen to him monologue all day. It’s something that’s kooky and uncanny and cool and awesome that you know every time you watch, you are going to enjoy.
